column3: The promised Day brings humbled, downcast eyes, directly paralleling the focus's future forced seeing.
God's knowledge of furtive eyes supports accountability, though not the delayed perception of judgment.
The divine names Hearing and Seeing are only a general background parallel.
Wrongdoers are deferred to a Day when eyes stare fixedly, closely matching delayed judgment-day perception.
Mary's veil is a local narrative image of concealment, not the focus's moral blindness.
God's Hearing and Seeing ground divine choice but do not develop human misguidance or final arrival.
The covering is removed and sight becomes sharp on that Day, an exact counterpart to belated clarity.
The declaration of disputed truth in the same passage supplies the truth whose rejection underlies the focus.
Given hearing, sight, and hearts fail to yield gratitude, explaining why capacities do not prevent present error.
It explicitly places wrongdoers in clear error after challenging their false objects of worship.
The immediately following warning names the Day of Regret while people remain heedless and unbelieving now.
Those seeking to mislead others ultimately mislead themselves without realizing it.
Deafness, blindness, and clear error directly frame the refusal of guidance despite its availability.
The woe against persistent lying sin offers a general punitive counterpart to the focus's wrongdoers.
Idols lead many astray, supplying a cause of the clear error named in the focus.
It uses the exact phrase clear error to describe a mistaken religious orientation.
Jesus's speech advances the local proof narrative but has no direct hearing, sight, or judgment link.
The disciplined, unerring gaze is a distant contrast to failed human perception.
Abraham identifies his audience and their ancestors as being in clear error.
The same passage rejects the false divine-son claim, the dispute whose deniers face the warned Day.
The brothers' mistaken accusation of their father is a limited ironic use of clear error.
Wrongdoers hear the message but use it to sustain a hostile interpretation, separating hearing from guidance.
The immediately preceding verse warns disbelieving factions of witnessing a tremendous Day.
The paired command to hear and see emphasizes complete divine knowledge, but not human belated recognition.
On the Day of Resurrection, disbelievers receive shame and evil, matching the focus's judgment setting.
Its contrast between what is and is not seen is too general to support the focus closely.
Hearing, sight, and hearts are divine gifts that people insufficiently acknowledge.
Leaders project the charge of clear error onto a prophet, exposing a recurrent reversal of judgment.
The immediate continuation states that all on earth return to God, completing the focus's coming-to-Us horizon.
Those disputing the Hour are in distant error, contrasted with believers who know its reality.
Hearing, sight, and hearts did not benefit a people who rejected God's signs, directly explaining failed perception.
The immediate call to worship God names the straight path opposed to the focus's clear error.
Dazzling lightning can overwhelm sight, but the physical image is only an indirect parallel.
Mockers question delayed punishment until the Day it arrives and cannot be turned away.
Mary's appeal for protection is unrelated to the focus's warning about wrongful misguidance.
The deceiving enemy is called manifestly misleading, but the narrative setting is otherwise remote.
The command to watch anticipates that opponents will later see the outcome.
God's just judgment and Hearing-Seeing are broad theological support rather than a close neighbour.
A community rejects unfamiliar truth because it has not heard it before, illustrating obstructed reception.
Lot's difficult day is an immediate crisis, not the eschatological day of the focus.
The boastful person will come to God alone, reinforcing the surrounding return-and-accountability sequence.
God hears and sees the confrontation, but the verse does not concern human guidance or final reckoning.
It warns of a Day when worldly means and intercession fail, and calls disbelievers wrongdoers.
The divinely decreed sign belongs to the local narrative but only indirectly prepares the later dispute.
Divine hearing and knowledge in seeking refuge are not closely related to delayed recognition.
God leaves hypocrites wandering blindly in their rebellion, a present counterpart to the focus's error.
Abraham's separation and reward do not materially develop the focus's themes.
The opponents are told they will eventually see, creating a present-versus-future contrast.
The Day when all are exposed before God is a close accountability parallel to coming to Him.
The book's divine origin is too general for this focus.
God sees all deeds and knows the unseen, providing the basis for eventual judgment.
Faith in the Last Day is a broad positive contrast without a direct perceptual or warning link.
Everyone in the heavens and earth comes to the Merciful as a servant, closely echoing coming to Us.
Wrongdoers follow desire without knowledge and have no guide, explaining their present misdirection.
The challenge to an unsupported claim of secret hearing is a distant reception-of-revelation parallel.
The crowd's accusation against Mary supplies local conflict but not the focus's judgment theme.
The question whether people fail to see confronts their inability to recognize impending reality.
Wrongdoers face humiliation at death for false speech and arrogant rejection of signs.
Abraham's withdrawal from idolaters is only a remote contrast to present misguidance.
Limited worldly knowledge leads people away from God's path, supporting the focus's diagnosis of error.
The believers' striving and success are not a close thematic neighbour.
The rebuke for irrational dispute is only loosely related to mistaken religious judgment.
Errant sight is mentioned within a different scene and offers little support for the focus.
God and the angels witness revelation, countering the disbelief at issue in the surrounding passage.
Every person comes alone on the Day of Resurrection, directly extending the focus's arrival before God.
Impressive appearance and speech conceal inner failure, showing sensory reception without true understanding.
God's unfailing promise of the hereafter provides the positive horizon against the focus's warning.
The accusation based on Mary's family reputation is local context but not a close conceptual link.
The condemned admit a warner came, falsely charged it with error, and thereby acknowledge their own error.
The enduring reward promised to the God-conscious supplies a broad contrast to wrongful loss.
False gods will disavow their worshippers and become opponents, developing the later reversal of false devotion.
All return to God to be informed of their deeds, while guidance remains distinct from others' error.
The virtues of the Helpers do not materially illuminate the focus.
The universal mission as bearer of warning explains why ignorance does not remove responsibility.
Pharaoh misled his people instead of guiding them, a concrete case of destructive leadership.
On that Day bodily witnesses speak to God, a close final-accountability counterpart to coming before Him.
The crowd's refusal to speak with an infant belongs to the local proof scene but is only indirect.
People in the Fire retrospectively confess that they were in clear error.
Rejected first guidance distorts hearts and eyes and leaves people wandering blindly.
Abraham identifies idols as unable to hear or see, contrasting false objects with the coming-to-God judgment.
Former misguidance before divine guidance is a remote positive contrast.
Humiliated wrongdoers are shown the Fire on the Day of Resurrection and remain in lasting punishment.
The oath by what people see is only a general reflection on visible and invisible evidence.
Choosing error over guidance and punishment over forgiveness makes the focus's moral diagnosis concrete.
On the Day when wrongdoers' excuses do not benefit them, they receive curse and an evil abode.
Jesus's moral commission is local context but does not directly bear on the focus's warning.
Both sides will eventually see which judgment is vindicated, though the Day is not explicit.
The Day of upheaval gathers every person without omission, a close final-arrival parallel.
Mary's provision from the palm tree is unrelated to the focus's themes.
The prophets' insight is a broad positive image of perception, without the focus's temporal reversal.
The people of the Blaze confess that truly hearing or reasoning would have prevented their fate.
Its condemnation of those farthest astray is a general punitive comparison with limited linkage.
Moses's separation from a defiantly sinful people is only a distant parallel to error and judgment.
The dazzled stare at the onset of resurrection closely matches compelled perception on the final Day.
The promise to admit believers among the righteous is a broad afterlife contrast only.
After the deed, idolaters recognize their error and seek mercy, an earlier-world counterpart to belated insight.
The sudden end of worldly adornment is a general warning but lacks the focus's perception motif.
Humans are made hearing and seeing as part of their trial, supplying the capacities implicated by the focus.
Its message reaching worshippers has little direct connection to delayed hearing, sight, or error.
Those blind in this world are blind and further astray in the Hereafter, directly linking present and final perception.
Wrongdoers see the Fire and wish to return rather than deny the signs, showing recognition that comes after consequence.
When they stand before their Lord, deniers are compelled to acknowledge that the meeting is true.
Wrongdoers rush forward on the Day with fixed stares, extending 14:42's image of powerless sight.
All are presented before their Lord in ranks, directly developing the focus's coming before God.
The criminals see the Fire, know they will fall into it, and find no escape.
The God-conscious are gathered to the Merciful on a Day, a positive counterpart to the focus's arrival before Him.
The criminals are driven thirsty to Hell, giving the adverse outcome of the same immediate surah horizon.
Destroyed generations cannot be perceived or heard, a sensory warning placed at the surah's close.
The Trumpet Day gathers sinners with altered, downcast appearance, reinforcing judgment-day exposure.
On that Day all follow the caller and voices are humbled, joining compelled hearing with final summons.
Faces are humbled before the Ever-Living Sustainer, and the wrongdoer fails.
When the true promise nears, disbelievers' eyes stare while they confess heedlessness and wrongdoing.
Disbelievers remain in doubt until the Hour comes suddenly or a barren Day overtakes them.
At the Trumpet blast, worldly ties cease and no one can question another, marking the final summons.
The Day criminals see the angels brings them no good news and exposes their condemned state.
The wrongdoer bites his hands on the Day, voicing regret over refusing the Messenger's path.
On the Day God calls people about their alleged partners, false devotion is publicly exposed.
The repeated call about alleged partners sharpens the judgment-day collapse of false claims.
Idolaters disown and curse one another on the Day of Resurrection before entering the Fire.
When the Hour arrives, the criminals fall into despair.
On the Day the Hour comes, criminals' false assessment of time continues their self-deception.
Criminals before their Lord confess, We have seen and heard, an exceptionally direct counterpart to 19:38.
Wrongdoers stand before their Lord blaming one another after the truth they rejected becomes manifest.
At the Trumpet blast, people emerge from graves and hasten toward their Lord.
The resurrected recognize that the Merciful's promise and the messengers' warning were true.
The soul's regret before God centers on neglect, mockery, and failure to heed guidance.
The Trumpet and resurrection bring all who are in the heavens and earth before their Lord's judgment.
Disbelievers are driven to Hell after the warning of messengers is recalled.
The approaching Day chokes hearts with anguish; wrongdoers have neither protector nor accepted intercessor.
God's enemies are gathered to the Fire and held in ordered ranks for judgment.
The bodily witnesses explain their testimony against their owners, making hidden wrongdoing audible at judgment.
The Hour comes suddenly while people remain unaware, matching the focus's present heedlessness.
God's dominion and judgment culminate in the Day the Hour is established, when falsehood loses.
Those who doubted the Hour are confronted with the reality they had dismissed as conjecture.
The Trumpet arrives with the threat fulfilled, introducing the Day that had been denied.
The command to listen for the caller's cry on the Day of emergence is a direct hearing-and-summons parallel.
People are called out on a Day of overwhelming horror after having turned away from warning.
With humbled eyes they emerge from graves and rush toward the caller.
All generations are gathered at a known appointed Day, reinforcing the certainty of universal return.
On the Day of severe exposure, people are called to prostrate but are unable.
Their humbled eyes and overwhelming humiliation result from refusing the call while they could still respond.
On the Day of presentation, no secret remains concealed, completing the focus's exposure before God.
Deniers are left in distraction until they meet the Day they were promised.
They emerge rapidly from graves toward their goal, immediately leading into 70:44's humbled eyes.
The Trumpet's blast begins a decisive Day of judgment.
That Day is hard for disbelievers and not easy, matching the focus's warning to wrongdoers.
When people see the Hour, worldly life appears as no more than a brief evening or morning.
The deafening blast initiates the Day when ordinary human bonds are abandoned.
When Hell is brought near, the human being remembers, but that late remembrance no longer benefits him.
People will certainly see the Blaze, making final perception unavoidable.
They will see it with the eye of certainty, the clearest contrast to present error.
